Diesel rationing could come within weeks and prices could top $4 a litre, says Saul Kavonic

MST Marquee's head of energy research, Saul Kavonic says fuel rationing could come into effect in Australia within weeks, and the price of diesel could top $4 a litre, if US President Donald Trump follows through with threats to ban US diesel exports.

Speaking to The Business' Kirsten Aiken, he says "the scope for the US to now ban diesel exports is probably the most worrying development we've seen in global fuel markets since the war began when it comes to Australia's vulnerability".
Australia is the world's largest importer of diesel, accounting for 10 per cent of the world's seaborne diesel imports to support our agricultural economy, according to Mr Kavonic.

"That makes us particularly vulnerable now, where diesel in particular is the tightest part of the market," he says."This is the kind of thing which could have to see Australia reconsider our demand management and rationing program potentially go to stage three and stage four."
"That makes us particularly vulnerable now, where diesel in particular is the tightest part of the market," he says.
"This is the kind of thing which could have to see Australia reconsider our demand management and rationing program potentially go to stage three and stage four."
Kirsten Aiken asks Mr Kavonic how quickly Australia might see the rationing.

"If the US does go down this path, particularly if they do it in a very severe way, I think we'll be looking at that in a matter of weeks, particularly if we don't see a de-escalation in the Middle East occuring at the same time," he says.
"And if that continues to escalate, plus a US export ban, that's the one situation which we were really fearing and hoping would not happen.
"And unfortunately, it could be on our doorstep."

Price of diesel — things could get hairy
Donald Trump might be about to send another shockwave through global energy markets.
According to Politico, America may impose a ban on the export of diesel as soon as this week.
There is division among members of Donald Trump’s cabinet on the issue, but he has publicly indicated support for some sort of restriction.
Energy Secretary Chris Wright says no blanket ban on exports is being considered, but they are looking at the "most efficient way to get more diesel into the US".
The motive is to try to bring record domestic diesel prices down which are hurting the ruling Republican party politically at home.
The midterm elections will take place in early November.
America is the world’s biggest exporter of diesel, and if it cuts off supply, it will send global prices surging.

The world is already dealing with a supply issue because Russia, which is usually the second biggest exporter of diesel, is currently heavily restricting its exports to deal with its own domestic pressures.
Its refining capability has been badly impacted by Ukrainian attacks on its energy infrastructure.
While in normal times Australia doesn’t import a lot of diesel from America, it has supplied us at crucial times this year.
Australia is the world leader in per-capita consumption of diesel, and our economy is heavily dependent on the fuel.
This could get hairy, quickly.
Price of diesel may rise further
Many across the country will be watching diesel prices today, as the United States looks to introduce an export ban.
According to Politico, the Trump administration is looking to ban diesel exports for 90 days to bring down energy prices.
As of 9pm AEST yesterday, the average price of diesel was nearly $2.92 a litre.

Key Event
'Bond market riot': US Treasury yields reach 19-year high
US Treasury yields have reached a new high not seen since 2007, as investors sell off government debt.
Treasury yields rose as high as 5.13% on Wednesday trading, closing at 5.11%.
It was the worst day in nearly 18 months for US government bonds, as the 10-year yield’s rise saw its sharpest one-day jump since April 9, 2025, a week after Trump’s liberation day tariffs.
NAB's Head of FX Strategy Ray Attrill calls this movement a "fresh bond market riot".

"Bond markets are back centre stage with sharp sell-offs across the US and European yield spectrums, the strength of US S&P Global PMIs a key catalyst and later compounded by a poorly received US Treasury 5-year note auction, which saw yields up through 5% for the first time since 2007," he says.

"Unhelpful to the cause has been a recovery in oil prices on renewed pessimism toward a US-Iran deal to re-open the Strait of Hormuz, and reports the US is preparing to ban diesel exports for 90 days.

"Risk sentiment has been sourced by the bond market riot, while the US dollar is stronger across the board as markets become more convinced about additional Fed rate hikes, with October now seen more likely than not for the next one."
Key Event
Half of young Australian adults now living with parents
With this latest data, one would hope young Aussies are getting on with their parents, as 50% of those aged 18 to 29 were still living at home in 2024.
That's up from 39% in 2001.

The data comes from this year's Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) annual survey, the largest longitudinal study of its kind in Australia, which follows the same 17,000 people each year to understand how our lives are changing.
It also found that, as a nation, we are more stressed about housing and money, tired, worried about our cognitive health, and half of us have jobs we're over-qualified for.
But the positive takeaways include high employment, more women holding university degrees, and our long-term relationships being in pretty good health.
